You have built your dataset and run your analysis (Phases 1-14). What remains
is the final step: getting your results safely out of DST.

Data from Statistics Denmark is microdata subject to GDPR. You **cannot** copy
raw data out - everything must go through DST's repatriation process, and the
precise rules live in DST's own guide.

::: {.callout-important}
**This page is only an overview. DST's own guide takes precedence - read and
re-read it.** [DST - Rules for repatriation of analysis results
→](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-hjemtagelse-af-analyseresultater)
:::

## What may leave DST?

**Yes:**

- Aggregated tables
- Graphs and figures
- Model output - coefficients, confidence intervals, p-values

**No:**

- Individual-level data in any form
- Small cells - see the threshold below
- Results that could identify individuals - directly or indirectly
- Screenshots or photographs of the screen. The ban on taking data out covers
  every route, [including images of the research machine
  →](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-arbejdet-med-mikrodata)

::: {.callout-note}
**Scripts are also repatriated via the process - not freely.** Code/scripts can
be repatriated, but go through the same process as result files.
:::

## Which cell size applies to you

DST's baseline is **at least 3 observations per cell**. Some registers are
stricter and require **at least 5**, and which rule applies to your project is
shown in the DDV App when the data is ordered. Check it there rather than
assuming.

This page uses **5** throughout, because it is the safe side of both rules and
because health register data is usually in the stricter group. If your project
is on the baseline of 3, nothing here breaks: you are simply reporting more
conservatively than required.

## A hidden number must not be possible to work out {#back-calculation}

Hiding the small cells is not enough on its own. DST's rules also say that a
hidden number must not be possible to work out again from the rest of what you
take home:

> "Observationer, som er blevet aggregeret eller på anden vis sløret eller
> fjernet i en tabel, graf eller figur, må ikke kunne udledes ved tilbageregning
> eller krydslæsning. Hvis dette er muligt, skal der aggregeres yderligere."

In English: observations that have been aggregated, blurred or removed in a
table, graph or figure must not be possible to derive by back calculation or by
reading tables against each other. If they can be, aggregate further. In plain
words: no subtracting your way back to a hidden number, within one table or
across tables.

The usual way it happens is a total. Take two rows of a Table 1 with an overall
column:

  | Age   | Overall | Exposed (N = 282) | Unexposed (N = 1,218) |
  | ----- | ------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
  | 70-89 | 165     | 35                | 130                   |
  | 90+   | 18      | 1                 | 17                    |

Only **1** exposed person is aged 90+, so you hide that number. But the row
still shows 18 overall and 17 unexposed, and 18 - 17 = 1. So you must hide **a
second number in the same row**, the 17. Now the column gives the 1 back
instead: the exposed column shows N = 282 and every other age group, so the
missing 1 is what is left over. So a number in the same column must go too, and
then one more to close the square:

  | Age   | Overall | Exposed (N = 282) | Unexposed (N = 1,218) |
  | ----- | ------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
  | 70-89 | 165     | ..                | ..                    |
  | 90+   | 18      | ..                | ..                    |

A reader can still see that the four hidden numbers add up to 165 and 18 across,
and to what is left of each column. But that fits every split from 0 to 18
exposed people aged 90+, so the 1 cannot be found.

The numbers you hide to protect a small one must not be small themselves. If you
hid a 1 and a 3 in the same column, a reader could still see from N that they
add up to 4, and 4 people is a small cell in its own right. Hide numbers so that
the hidden ones in each row and each column add up to at least 5. Here they do:
165 and 18 across, 36 and 147 down.

Usually the better answer is the one DST's rule itself points to: **merge
categories** ("aggregeres yderligere"). Here a single `70+` group would leave
nothing to hide.

Where to look for numbers that give a hidden one back:

- **Totals, overall columns and N in the header.** Each of them makes a sum that
  one hidden number can be subtracted from. A row or column with a total needs
  either no hidden number or at least two, and the hidden ones together must
  come to at least 5. As the example shows, the second one often pulls in more.
- **Percentages.** A percentage is a number of people in disguise: 0.4% of 282
  is 1 person. If you hide a count, hide its percentage too.
- **The same people in two tables.** If Table 1 shows 18 people aged 90+ and
  Table 2 shows the 17 unexposed among them, the two tables together give the 1
  back. Check every table you take home together, and the ones you took home
  earlier.
- **Subgroups and sensitivity analyses.** If the main analysis has 120 people
  and a sensitivity analysis on almost the same people has 118, a reader knows
  that 2 people are in one and not in the other. When the difference is below
  5, do not give both sizes exactly. One way is to round them, for example to
  the nearest 10; another is to give only the main analysis' size. The same
  goes for the exclusion boxes in a flowchart ([Phase 10 - Build your study
  population](build-study-population.qmd)).
- **The mark you use for a hidden number.** When you hide some numbers and show
  the rest exactly, a mix of marks gives the small one away: if it says `<5` and
  the numbers hidden to protect it say `..`, a reader knows which one is 1 to 4,
  and next to a total that narrows it down, sometimes to a single value. Give
  every hidden number in a table the same neutral mark, such as `..` (a hidden
  17 is not `<5` anyway). Saying in the methods that counts below 5 are hidden
  is fine, since DST's threshold is public.

## NB: min, max, percentiles and median can point to one person

`min`, `max`, percentiles and `median` reproduce concrete values from the
dataset - a minimum or maximum value *is* one person's actual figure. Only
report them if **at least 5 people have that value**; otherwise the figure can
point to a single individual.

If you are unsure about a descriptive table with min, max, percentiles or
median, check the threshold in DST's guide or with your data manager before
repatriating it.

## NB: missing values (NA) count too

A missing value is also a cell. If a category has **fewer than 5 missing**, that
figure may not be repatriated either. Solutions: impute, merge categories, drop
the category - or another solution agreed with your data manager.

Make a quick overview of missing values, so you see the small cells immediately
instead of adding figures up in your head:

```r
colSums(is.na(df)) # number of NAs per column - spot any 1–4 at a glance
table(df$category, useNA = "always") # shows NA as its own category (otherwise hidden)
```

`table()` hides NA by default - `useNA = "always"` forces the NA row out. See
[Phase 7 - `table()` hides NA](inspect-data.qmd).

## How it works

The repatriation itself happens via **"Hjemtag Filer"** in the DDV app. The
system automatically scans for potential microdata and flags risks. If a file is
flagged, you add a comment that precisely describes what the file contains and
why it is aggregated. Use **descriptive filenames**
(`table1_descriptive_n500.csv`) - not generic names like `output.csv`.

The full step-by-step process and the rules in force are in [DST's
guide](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-hjemtagelse-af-analyseresultater) -
follow it.

## Checklist before uploading

- [ ] No individual-level data - only aggregated results
- [ ] All cells ≥ 5 observations
- [ ] No hidden number can be worked out from a total, a percentage, another
      table or an earlier export - merge categories, or hide more numbers so
      the hidden ones in each row and column add up to at least 5
- [ ] Hidden numbers share one mark (e.g. `..`), so the small one cannot be
      told apart from those hidden to protect it
- [ ] Min, max, percentiles, median: at least 5 people behind each value
- [ ] No category has 1--4 missing (NA) - impute, merge or drop
- [ ] Descriptive filenames; scripts clean - no microdata in the code
- [ ] File type is on DST's approved list: spreadsheets (xlsx, csv), text, HTML,
      PDF, Word, code (R, SAS, Stata), images (png, jpg, pdf), presentations

## You have completed the full process

When your results have been repatriated, you have gone all the way - from
research question and cohort to analysis-ready dataset and publication-ready
results.
